False scad (Caranx rhonchus) is a commercially important carangid distributed along the eastern Atlantic coast, from Morocco to Angola. Field surveys indicate that this species attains a maximum recorded body length of 60 centimeters [Li = 60 centimeters], a size typical of mid-sized members of the genus Caranx. The weight-length relationship derived from specimens collected in Senegalese waters suggests that an individual reaching this ultimate length would have a corresponding wet body mass of approximately 2665 grams [Wwi = approximately 2665 grams], reflecting the robust, laterally compressed body morphology characteristic of this genus. Juveniles and sub-adults are commonly encountered over sandy substrates and in estuarine environments, where they feed predominantly on small crustaceans and early-stage teleosts. As individuals grow and approach their asymptotic size, their diet shifts increasingly toward larger pelagic prey items, including engraulids and clupeids, a trophic transition that is accompanied by notable changes in gill raker spacing and jaw morphology. The species exhibits a relatively fast growth rate during the first two years of life, with length increments slowing considerably after the onset of gonadal maturation.

Histological staging of ovaries reveals asynchronous oocyte development, with the simultaneous presence of perinucleolar, vitellogenic, and hydrated oocytes in gravid females, indicating batch spawning capability over an extended reproductive period. Spawning appears to be most intense during the warmer months when sea surface temperatures are elevated, though some reproductive activity has been documented year-round in lower latitudes. The onset of sexual maturity at this modest body size suggests a life-history strategy that prioritizes early reproductive output.

Individual females have been recorded releasing up to 2712 eggs daily [Ri = up to 2712 eggs daily], a remarkably high fecundity that compensates for the substantial mortality experienced during the planktonic egg and larval stages. The daily reproductive rate is influenced by female size, with larger, older individuals producing more oocytes per batch compared to first-time spawners. This high fecundity is characteristic of many tropical and subtropical carangids, which typically exhibit extended spawning seasons and high instantaneous reproductive rates to overcome the low survival probabilities faced by pelagic early life stages in a predator-rich environment.

The early life history of Caranx rhonchus begins with the release of small, transparent, pelagic eggs that have an average diameter of 1 millimeter. Based on this egg size, the wet weight at birth is calculated to be 0.000523 grams [Wwb = 0.000523 grams], a minute mass that reflects the limited yolk reserves available to the developing embryo. The transition to first feeding is a critical period marked by high mortality due to starvation and predation. Larvae captured in plankton tows show rapid development of the jaw apparatus and eyes, enabling effective prey capture shortly after mouth opening. The duration of the pelagic larval phase is influenced by water temperature and food availability.

Maximum lifespan in False scad has been determined through analysis of otolith growth increments from specimens collected across its geographic range. Under the thermal conditions typical of its subtropical habitat, at 19.2 °C [T = 19.2 °C], the oldest documented individuals reach approximately 10 years [am = approximately 10 years] of age. This longevity is moderate among carangids, with some larger congeners such as Caranx ignobilis living considerably longer, while smaller species may complete their life cycle in fewer than six years.
